text: Force Z: The Sinking of the Prince of Wales and Repulse
On the 2nd of December 1941, two of the most powerful warships in the world came up the Johore Strait and anchored at Singapore, and the island thrilled to see them.
Eight days later both ships were on the seabed off Kuantan, sunk by aircraft in under two hours, and 840 of their men were dead.

Force Z would go to Singapore with no carrier — a fact known in London, and accepted there, because the gesture was the point: the ships had been publicly announced, and their arrival was itself the message.

When Churchill let it be known that the two capital ships were coming, Japan reinforced its air groups in Indochina with dozens more bombers, and trained their crews, for the first time in the war, specifically in killing fast ships under way at sea.
He sailed anyway, in strict radio silence, counting on surprise and on weather — a curtain of rain and cloud under which a fleet might move unseen.
It was exactly the target his force existed to strike, and he turned north to strike it, still in radio silence, telling no one ashore where he was going.
One torpedo struck her aft, on the port side, exactly where the outer propeller shaft left the hull — the single most destructive hit of the day.

At about twenty past twelve the last torpedo wave caught Repulse in a pincer, aircraft attacking from both sides at once so that dodging one spread of torpedoes turned her into the path of another; four or five struck home within minutes.
Tennant ordered his men over the side, and at twelve thirty-three Repulse rolled over and went down.
At one eighteen, the flagship sank.
At one eighteen, at that very minute, the Buffaloes of 453 Squadron arrived over the oil and wreckage.
Eight hundred and forty were not: 513 from Repulse and 327 from Prince of Wales, among them Captain Leach, who went down with his ship, and Admiral Phillips, who went down with his.

The two ships were the first capital ships in history, steaming and fighting in the open sea, to be sunk by air power alone — eighty-eight Japanese aircraft had done it, for the loss of three of their own.
In 2014 the wrecks were reported extensively damaged by explosives used by scrap-metal dealers.

Beside the British officers at the rail stood a young officer of the Japanese destroyer Akebono, Sub Lieutenant Takumi Kitamura, helping to honour the same dead: the navies of the two countries that fought over those ships, laying wreaths together in the same water.
